clinicalPearls: The severe X-linked form (myotubular myopathy, MTM1) presents in affected males at birth with profound hypotonia, weakness, respiratory failure and often a history of polyhydramnios and reduced fetal movements
Autosomal dominant (DNM2) and recessive (BIN1) centronuclear forms are generally milder with later onset and slower progression
Ophthalmoplegia and ptosis are common and are a useful clinical clue, alongside a long face and proximal weakness
Muscle biopsy hallmark is centrally placed nuclei in a high proportion of fibres, often with a central zone of oxidative enzyme activity surrounded by a pale halo, resembling fetal myotubes
Male infants with the X-linked form frequently have macrosomia, long digits and elongated face
Creatine kinase is usually normal or mildly elevated
Carrier females for MTM1 variants may occasionally show mild or asymmetric weakness
reference.pathophysiology: Centronuclear myopathies are congenital myopathies characterised by centrally located nuclei in muscle fibres. The severe X-linked form is caused by loss-of-function variants in MTM1, which encodes myotubularin, a phosphoinositide phosphatase important for membrane trafficking and the organisation of the triad and T-tubule system. Autosomal dominant disease is usually caused by DNM2 (dynamin 2) variants and recessive disease by BIN1 (amphiphysin 2) variants; all converge on disturbed membrane remodelling and excitation-contraction coupling. The resulting maldevelopment of the sarcotubular system impairs contractile function and, in severe cases, arrests fibres at a myotube-like stage.
additionalInvestigations: Muscle biopsy demonstrating central nuclei and perinuclear oxidative staining patterns
Genetic testing of MTM1, DNM2 and BIN1 with appropriate X-linked inheritance analysis
Respiratory function assessment, critical in neonates with the X-linked form
Ophthalmological assessment for ptosis and ophthalmoplegia
Electromyography and, where relevant, hepatic and coagulation monitoring in severe MTM1 disease
redFlags: Neonatal respiratory failure requiring immediate ventilatory support
Signs of hepatic peliosis or bleeding described in severe X-linked disease
Progressive hypoventilation in older children with dominant or recessive forms
reference.prognosis: The severe X-linked form carries high early mortality from respiratory failure, though intensive respiratory support has improved survival in some cases. Autosomal dominant and recessive centronuclear forms are typically slowly progressive and compatible with prolonged survival, with disability determined mainly by limb and respiratory muscle involvement.
pitfalls: Failing to arrange urgent respiratory support in a hypotonic newborn with the X-linked form
Overlooking ptosis and ophthalmoplegia that point toward centronuclear myopathy
Assuming a female carrier is unaffected when mild manifestations can occur
Interpreting central nuclei as regenerating fibres rather than the primary pathology
management: No curative therapy exists, so provide supportive care, with neonatal mechanical ventilation for respiratory failure in the severe X-linked MTM1 form
Support nutrition with gastrostomy feeding where bulbar weakness impairs feeding
Institute proactive respiratory surveillance with airway clearance, non-invasive ventilation and prompt treatment of chest infections
Provide physiotherapy, occupational therapy, orthoses and management of contractures and scoliosis
Refer to ophthalmology for ptosis and ophthalmoplegia, using ptosis props or surgery
Monitor for hepatic peliosis, haemorrhage and coagulopathy in MTM1 disease
Offer genetic counselling and family or carrier testing given X-linked MTM1, autosomal dominant DNM2 and recessive BIN1 inheritance
Coordinate a multidisciplinary neuromuscular team and consider emerging gene-directed therapies within trials
